title: Why New Zealand Cannot Crack India's Death Bowling in T20I Series
excerpt: Bracewell cites 26 and 23 runs conceded in the last two overs of the Christchurch matches as India lead 2-0, with Wellington now a must-win for the hosts.
body:
• India lead the five-match T20I series 2-0 after two wins in Christchurch; the third match is in Wellington, where New Zealand must win to keep the series alive.
  • Michael Bracewell pointed to India's bowling at the death: New Zealand were restricted to 26 runs in the last two overs while making 225 in the first match and 23 runs in the last two overs while making 180 in the second.
  • The second match still turned at the other end too: India recovered from 70 for 5 to chase 181, with Tilak Varma unbeaten on 51 off 26, after New Zealand reprieved four batters.
  • Bracewell's remedy is not a rebuild: do what New Zealand do well for a touch longer and be clinical in the key moments India have won so far.

New Zealand's problem in this series is narrow, measurable and, so far, unsolved. Ahead of the third T20I in Wellington, all-rounder Michael Bracewell identified India's bowling at the death as a central reason the hosts trail 2-0, after totals of 225 and 180 in Christchurch still proved insufficient in the series reported by Rediff via Sports Wire Live.

The death-overs numbers

Bracewell's point was specific. In the first two matches India conceded only 26 runs and then 23 runs in the final two overs of New Zealand's innings, in games that were otherwise high scoring. Holding a batting side to 23 to 26 runs across the last 12 balls, twice in a row, removes the late surge that normally turns a competitive T20 total into a commanding one. New Zealand posted 225 for 4 in the opener and 180 for 5 in the second match, according to the match reports, but in neither case did the innings finish with momentum.

The second innings in Christchurch showed how India closed it out. ESPNcricinfo's match report recorded New Zealand at 180 for 5, with Glenn Phillips making 70 off 43 and Bevon Jacobs 58 in a 116-run fourth-wicket stand, before Arshdeep Singh, who finished with 2 for 33, removed Phillips with two overs to go. Phillips and Jacobs had accelerated through the middle, taking 11 off Axar Patel in the 15th over, 18 off Bhuvneshwar Kumar in the 16th and 12 in the 17th, which makes the late containment more telling: India regained control precisely when New Zealand needed to break away.

"It's just about being clinical in those key moments, and India have been, and I guess we'd like to have a couple of those situations back."

— Michael Bracewell, New Zealand all-rounder

Only half the story: New Zealand's own death bowling

The mirror image has hurt New Zealand just as much. In the first match, India were 167 for 5 in 14.3 overs chasing 226, before Naman Dhir struck an unbeaten 42 off 15 balls and captain Shreyas Iyer made 42 off 28 to complete a four-wicket win, CricTracker reported. In the second, India fell to 70 for 5 chasing 181, and still won with a ball to spare. ESPNcricinfo recorded Tilak Varma unbeaten on 51 off 26, Dhir making 31, and Dhir and Nitish Kumar Reddy scoring 57 between them at nearly two runs a ball.

Fielding compounded the bowling problem in that second chase. ESPNcricinfo reported New Zealand reprieved four India batters, including Dhir dropped by Jacobs at the start of the 13th over when India still needed 97 off 48 balls, the moment the report identified as the start of the turnaround. Captain Mitchell Santner, who took 4 for 21, said the small stuff of dropped catches and misfields had cost his side and that New Zealand could easily have been 2-0 up instead.

Fine margins Bracewell keeps returning to

Bracewell singled out one ball of his own: a six Dhir hit off him over deep mid-wicket, just over the fielder's head at the 85-metre boundary at the end of the 14th over of the second match, turning the over into a 15-run over. If Dhir mistimes it slightly, Bracewell said, it becomes a wicket. He also noted India's powerplay threat, with Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma looking for hot starts, and credited the middle-overs spin of Santner and himself with slowing India down before the death overs decided both games.

What Wellington requires

Bracewell's prescription was continuity, not change: a complete performance, doing what New Zealand do well for a touch longer, and taking the key moments that have gone India's way. With three matches left and India needing one more win to seal the series, Wellington is a must-win for the hosts. The evidence of the first two matches suggests the contest will again be decided in the last two overs of each innings, the phase India have controlled with the ball and New Zealand have not.
